title: A Review of Crack Initiation and Propagation Characteristics of Cast Steels: Trends for Enabling the Reliable Use of Steel Castings
abstract: Abstract Steel castings are used in a wide range of industries, but there is a general shortage of accessible data on both crack initiation and propagation characteristics pertinent to their design for fatigue applications. The present study reviews literature data on the initiation and propagation characteristics of cast steels and illustrates some useful trends for designing with steel castings. Crack propagation rate and threshold data are framed within guidelines from flaw assessment procedures, indicating that codified values offering reasonably conservative guidance for wrought and welded structures can also do so for steel castings. Crack initiation data for a range of carbon, low-alloy, and high-alloy steels are framed within life estimation methods developed predominantly from wrought steels, and a modification to a previously established regression relationship is proposed, resulting in largely reasonable life predictions for cast steels. The compatibility of the approach with a previously developed generalized fatigue assessment procedure is also illustrated, highlighting its potential to integrate within stress-based frameworks.

sections.heading: Introduction and Background
paragraphs: Steel castings are widely used in the transportation, 1  materials processing, 2  power generation, 3  agriculture, 4  and mining industries, 5  with additional applications still being realized. 6 ,  7 ,  8 – 9  Despite the widespread use of castings in engineering applications, there is a general shortage of fatigue data available for design. Fatigue and fracture data for wrought steels can be readily found in a variety of reliable sources and, while not a substitute for component-level fatigue testing or experience, provide designers a reasonable starting point. While the design engineer can generally find the necessary fatigue parameters needed to compute fatigue life for a wrought component via stress life, strain life, or damage-tolerant design methodologies, the designer is often forced to rely on rules of thumb and experience where castings are concerned. This lack of fatigue data presents a challenge to both foundries and design engineers 10  and at times consternation for end users. As such, the present study seeks to utilize literature data for steel castings to arrive at some generalizations regarding crack initiation and propagation characteristics that may be of use to both design engineers and potential users of steel castings.

Virtually, all real materials contain quality details, whether in the form of shrinkage porosity or inclusions. Since “quality detail” is a newer term and likely less familiar to the technical community than the more commonly used “defect,” additional description of its meaning and motivation for use is warranted. The term quality detail is used purposefully to describe something that is relatively small and may or may not be acceptable with respect to the ability of the component to meet specified quality and performance requirements. The term is used in lieu of defect, flaw, or anomaly, which imply a fault that will inhibit the ability of the component to meet specified performance requirements and warrants corrective action. The distinction is important when considering that perfect materials do not exist (at least not in common engineering practice). For example, a bridge would not be considered defective because of a slag inclusion in a cover plate weld unless the slag inclusion compromised the ability of the structure to support a specified volume of traffic. Whether a particular quality detail will ultimately drive the cyclic performance of the part depends on a variety of factors, such as the stress state in the vicinity of the detail, loading history, section properties, and proximity of the detail to the surface. Once the presence of a quality detail is known or estimated, either from nondestructive evaluation or through simulation, its influence on resulting fatigue performance can be analyzed. Several methodologies have been proposed in this area, ranging from finite element models coupled to solidification simulations or nondestructive evaluation results 11 , 12  to analytical LEFM solutions based on a simplified crack geometry or effective area of the quality detail. 13 ,  14 – 15  However, analysis of the influence of the quality detail requires that either the relevant fatigue properties of the material be known or a reasonable method available to estimate them. For wrought steels, the designer can turn to several detailed sources for such fatigue data 16 , 17  or virtually any standard engineering textbook. 18 , 19  In lieu of handbook or test data, the designer can also turn to various regression relationships such as those proposed by Manson, 20  Meggiolaro and Castro, 21  Socie et al., 22  and Roessle and Fatemi. 23  Designers intending to utilize cast steels have comparatively fewer options but can turn to dedicated sources such as the Steel Castings Handbook. 24

The authors are aware of only a handful of published reviews pertaining to the fatigue properties of cast steels. 25 , 26  While the investigations by Stephens et al. 27 , 28  still represent one of the most extensive investigations on crack initiation and propagation characteristics for a range of cast steels, other more recent landmark works, such as that of Nagel, 29  also include extensive analysis of the cyclic behavior of cast steels. The present study seeks to utilize these prior works and others to provide an up to date and relevant review of steel casting initiation and propagation properties within a useful and accessible framework for the technical community. All the data in the present study have either been compiled from tabulated data where available or digitized in the case that tabulated values were not available. For clarity, symbols from all equations are defined at the end of the paper.

sections.heading: Fatigue Crack Growth Rates
paragraphs: The aforementioned equations were originally proposed as an upper bound on experimental crack growth data for various wrought ferrite-pearlite (ASTM A36, A302, A537), martensitic (HY-80, HY-130, 10Ni-Cr-Mo-Co), and austenitic (304, 305, 316) steels and form the basis for the following cast steel comparisons. While the equations are not exhaustive with respect to all the design curves available in various FFS codes, they provide a well-established benchmark to which cast steel literature data can be compared. As much of the older literature crack growth data cannot be reliably digitized for quantitative purposes and the transition point between the three regions of the Paris curve is often not tabulated in the literature, comparisons made with digitized data are predominantly qualitative. To distinguish the different steel types and compare to the upper bound equations, the cast steel data are sorted into three primary categories: ferrite-pearlite, martensitic, or austenitic. Notably, while several steels are referred to by ASTM designation consistent with the original source, it should not be inferred that a particular grade or composition is always produced to a particular microstructure. Microstructure can vary within the same grade based on composition and heat treatment as well as through the section thickness due to variations in cooling rate, particularly in thicker sections. The microstructure was not reported in all studies and therefore was either excluded from the analysis or inferred based on the alloy designation (if provided) or its strength. Data are restricted to long crack growth in ambient, non-aggressive environments consistent with the experimental conditions in which the upper bound equations were derived.

Figure  2  compares the fatigue crack growth data for austenitic cast steels from the literature dataset against the Barsom upper bound for austenitic stainless steels (note that the CF8 and 21 Cr 8 Ni alloys are primarily austenitic but can contain up to 40% ferrite 37 ). The data exhibit appreciable scatter relative to the ferrite-pearlite dataset in Figure  1 , wherein fatigue crack growth rates at a given stress intensity range for the same alloy (CF8M) differ by more than an order of magnitude. While the scatter indicates that the Barsom austenitic upper bound would estimate grossly conservative estimates with respect to some of the experimental data, it still approximates the upper bound and thus appears suitable for austenitic cast steels as well. The findings, should however, be considered in the context of the small dataset, and additional crack growth data for cast austenitic steels in ambient environments would help provide a stronger trend. Figure 2 Fatigue crack growth data for various austenitic cast steels compared to Barsom upper bound (solid blue line). Note that the designations in the legend do not imply an austenitic microstructure for a given grade/composition.

Figure  3  compares the fatigue crack growth data for martensitic cast steels from the literature dataset against the Barsom martensitic upper bound. The data include both low alloy (C-Mn, Mn-Mo, 8630) and high alloy (stainless steels CA6NM and 17-4PH), all of which remain under the Barsom martensitic upper bound with the exception of one C-Mn data point at 90 MPa*sqrt(m), which is close to the transition to region III crack growth. The data indicate a similar trend to that observed for the ferrite-pearlite steels in Figure  1 , wherein the slope of the data is generally steeper than that indicated by the Barsom martensitic upper bound. However, the fatigue crack growth rates still remain conservatively below this limit and suggest that the Barsom upper bound equations can also offer reasonable approximations for martensitic cast steels. Figure 3 Fatigue crack growth data for various martensitic cast steels compared to Barsom upper bound (solid red line). Note that the designations in the legend do not imply a martensitic microstructure for a given grade/composition.

While steel castings can generally be grouped by microstructure in the same manner as wrought steels, it is worth illustrating that conservative crack growth rate estimates can be achieved in a more general sense. Figure  4  illustrates the compilation of the fatigue crack growth data for ferrite-pearlite (Figure  1 ), austenitic (Figure  2 ), and martensitic (Figure  3 ) cast steels compared with the most conservative design curve outlined in BS 7910 38  (load ratio greater than or equal to R=0.5 plus two standard deviations). Although the conservatism could be considered excessive for the majority of the data points, the illustration is valuable in that the design curve encompasses the cast steel data over a wide range of stress intensities regardless of alloy type. Thus, while the Barsom upper bound correlations provide reasonably conservative approximations for ferrite-pearlite, martensitic, and austenitic cast steels, the designer also has the choice of opting for the more conservative design curves in BS 7910. Although the present comparisons do not indicate that the Barsom equations or BS 7910 design curves are universally suitable for all cast steels, the trend illuminated by the present dataset indicates that well-established fatigue crack growth curves developed from wrought steels can produce reasonable estimates for cast steels. It should, however, be reiterated that the data presented represent fatigue crack growth rates in ambient, non-aggressive environments, and caution should be exercised in any extrapolation of these findings to other conditions without additional experimental data. Figure 4 Ferrite-pearlite, martensitic, and austenitic cast steels compared to BS 7910 design curve for R ≥ 0.5 plus two standard deviations. The design curve serves as a reasonable upper bound on the cast steel fatigue crack growth data regardless of alloy type.

Tabulated Paris constants are summarized in Table  1 . Paris constants were not tabulated if they were not reported in the original study or if the data could not be adequately digitized for quantitative regression.

Although the majority of the crack growth rate data is from presumably sound castings (though this is not always stated explicitly), there are some studies that have studied crack growth through unsound material. Heuler et al. conducted crack growth tests on a low-alloy cast steel (2¼% Cr 1%Mo) containing hot tears, concluding that the average crack growth rate was comparable to that of the sound material and that closed hot tears warrant little consideration from a fracture mechanics perspective. 46  Selby reached a similar conclusion for a “partially unsound” 3½% Ni cast steel, which exhibited comparable fatigue crack growth and threshold characteristics to the sound material 26  though the specific quality detail was not reported. While the two studies may not be considered as comprehensive representations for the various quality details, geometries, and alloy systems present in steel castings, the trend lends value to the compilation of sound data and indicates that, at least with regard to fatigue crack growth, steel castings exhibit a degree of tolerance for the presence of quality details. Such tolerance is beneficial not only to ensure the casting meets its specified performance requirements but also to maintain its cost-effectiveness by avoiding unnecessary repairs of quality details that do not hinder performance.

Notably, fatigue crack propagation data pertaining to environments other than ambient conditions (room temperature air), largely reported for stainless steels for pressure water reactor (PWR) and hydraulic turbine runner applications, were not included in the present study. However, additional data for non-ambient conditions has been published, and in addition to SAE 0030 in air at -34°C, SAE 0050A in air at -45°, C-Mn in air at -45°C, Mn-Mo in air at -45°C, and AISI 8630 in air at -45°C 57 can be found for several other common cast steels. Investigations have been conducted for CF8M (ASTM A351) at -269°C, 58  CF8/CF8M in air at 300°C, 59  CF8M/CF8A in water at 316°C, 60  SCS5 (CA6NM) in water at ambient temperature, 61  CF8A in water at 232  and 288°C, 62  ASTM A27 at 100°C to 250°C in water and air, 63  CF3 in water at 288°C, 64 CF8M in air and water at 320°C, 52  21Cr-8Ni in air and water at 300°C, 48  ASTM A216 at 150°C in air, water, and brine, 65  ASTM A297 in air at 927°C, 66  ASTM A743 (CA6NM) in water, 67  and 1CrMoV in air at 538°C and 550°C. 68 Correlations between the non-ambient cast steel fatigue crack growth data and relevant non-ambient design curves such as those stipulated in the ASME BPVC will be addressed in future investigations.

sections.heading: Fatigue Crack Growth Thresholds
paragraphs: Although the environmental definitions provided for BS 7910 deviate from the ambient laboratory conditions in which the cast steel data were generated, the threshold guidelines in BS 7910 provide a useful, conservative approximation similar to that illustrated for fatigue crack growth rates. Ambiguity in threshold values at negative stress ratios complicates the inclusion of literature data in which it is not explicitly specified whether the threshold value is based on the full or positive portion of the stress range. Some studies indicate that the positive stress range can result in non-conservative threshold estimates at negative stress ratios (i.e., the threshold determined using only the positive stress range under compressive loading can be lower than the threshold under tension loading only). 70  To avoid complications in the consideration of negative stress ratios, only threshold values determined at positive stress ratios are included.

Figure  5  summarizes fatigue crack growth threshold values for both wrought and cast steels across positive stress ratios against increasingly conservative guidelines. The data have been grouped broadly to only distinguish cast steels from wrought steels, and no distinction is made between the type of steel. The wrought data tabulated from 72  and 73  include a wide range of carbon, low-alloy, and high-alloy steels, which serve as an additional qualitative benchmark. The ASME BPVC VIII, BPVC XI, and BS 7910 guidelines are represented by the red, black, and blue lines in order of generally increasing conservatism. The ASME BPVC VIII relation is expectedly conservative for wrought steels but also encompasses most of the cast steel data (approximately 90%). The more conservative ASME BPVC XI threshold values encompass a greater portion of the data (approximately 98%). Only one cast steel lies below the BPVC XI relation with a threshold value of 4.28 MPa*sqrt(m) against the 4.62 MPa*sqrt(m) value determined by the BPVC XI relation, from a postmortem investigation of a thick-walled C-Mn that failed during service. 44  The BS 7910 curve is the most conservative and bounds all cast steel data points. The trends must again be considered in the context of the relatively small dataset relative to the amount of wrought fatigue crack growth data in the literature, particularly when considering the scatter associated with fatigue crack growth testing. 74  However, the findings again offer the designer a degree of choice in the selection of a fatigue crack growth threshold when designing with steel castings, wherein guidance provided by ASME BPVC Sec. VIII and XI can be considered largely conservative, but guidance provided by BS 7910 can be used for additional conservatism. It should be emphasized that the findings pertain to long cracks consistent with those measured in typical compact tension specimens per ASTM-E647 and should not be extrapolated to short cracks, which typically exhibit lower threshold values. Figure 5 Fatigue crack growth threshold vs. stress ratio for cast (circles) and wrought (squares) steels. The solid red, black, and blue lines denote thresholds for the ASME BPVC Sec. VIII, ASME BPVC Sec. XI, and BS 7910. Note that for the ASME BPVC, a cutoff was implemented at R=0.17 to provide a smooth transition between the constant and stress ratio-dependent thresholds.

sections.heading: Initiation Life and Estimation Methods
paragraphs: Figure  6  summarizes the strain life curves compiled from literature for several cast carbon, low-alloy, and high-alloy steels. All data shown in Figure  6  were generated under fully reversed axial loading in ambient conditions. The data exhibit appreciable scatter, but some particular outliers are present and warrant additional clarification. The study on AISI 8630 by Sigl et al. 84  utilized samples that were intentionally cast to contain varying degrees of porosity. Similarly, the study on Mn-modified 8630 by Dittmer and Mitchell 85 utilized samples extracted from a 7-ft-diameter, 6-in-thick gear casting, and it was noted that a pronounced dendritic structure and internal porosity were present. Consequently, the cyclic behavior of the 8630 in both of these studies deviates from the majority of reported 8630 data generated from sound material. Tabulated values used to construct the strain life curves shown in Figure  6  are provided in Table  3 . Values not reported in the source are denoted with superscripts and were either calculated from the compatibility equations using values that were reported, determined via regression if the elastic and plastic strain amplitudes were explicitly reported, or excluded if neither method was possible. To reduce uncertainty associated with the calculated values in subsequent life predictions, the digitized experimental data points were used when comparing calculated and actual fatigue lives. Alloy designations are kept consistent with those used in the source. Figure 6 Strain life curves computed from literature data for cast steels. It was not explicitly stated what form all 724 steels used to develop the above equations were, but it is assumed that the majority were in wrought form with some welds based on the listed references. For clarity, both relationships are referred to subsequently by their respective authors.

Using the Roessle/Fatemi and Meggiolaro/Castro relationships, life predictions were generated for each specimen at the experimental strain amplitude in the cast steel dataset. Figure  7  and Figure  8  compare the predicted and actual lives for the cast steel dataset utilizing the Roessle/Fatemi relationship (Figure  7 ) and the Meggiolaro/Castro relationship (Figure  8 ). It should be reiterated that each data point on the plot corresponds to an experimental data point (one specimen) rather than a data point calculated from the strain life curve so that the majority of the cast steel data could be utilized without regard to the quality of the fits used to determine the strain life parameters in Table  3 . Consequently, some additional scatter is expected relative to using the experimentally determined strain life curve but does not convolute the observed trends. Scatter bands above and below the equality line correspond to life factors of 3, 5, and 10. Generally, both relationships generate predictions within the 10x life bands but predominantly overestimate the experimental cast steel fatigue lives. The Meggiolaro/Castro relationship produces slightly more conservative answers, but neither relationship appears directly suitable for cast steels. Overestimation of the cast steel fatigue lives using relationships developed from wrought steels is not an unexpected trend given the reductions reported in the unnotched rotating-bending fatigue strength between cast steels and wrought steels heat treated to the same strength. 99 Mitchell similarly concluded from axial fatigue tests that cyclic correlations developed for wrought steels tend to overpredict fatigue lives for castings, 94  and Figure  8  and Figure  9  corroborate this trend for a broader range of cast steels. It should not be concluded from the comparisons that one processing route is superior or inferior to the other, as this can only be determined in the context of specified performance requirements (which are absent here), as well as cost, manufacturability, etc. The present comparison does, however, reinforce the need for a more reasonable approximation relationship suitable for cast steels. Figure 7 Predicted vs. experimental reversals to failure for cast steels using the Roessle/Fatemi relationship. Scatter bands indicate life factors of 3, 5, and 10. Each data point represents one experimental specimen. Figure 8 Predicted vs. experimental reversals to failure for cast steels using the Meggiolaro/Castro relationship. Scatter bands indicate life factors of 3, 5, and 10. Each data point represents one experimental specimen. Figure 9 (a) Predicted vs. experimental cyclic strength coefficient (K'). (b) Predicted vs. experimental cyclic strain hardening coefficient (n’). Note that n’ is a constant with the constant fatigue ductility and strength exponents.

No attempt is made to distinguish differences in notch sensitivity between the normalized, quenched and tempered 8630 tested in the Blair study and the various other cast steels for evaluation. It will be shown subsequently that reasonable predictions are achieved despite this omission. It should also be emphasized that the use of the quantitative standard proposed by Blair et al. does not imply that a severity level of 3 in a radiographic standard such as ASTM-E186 106  will necessarily result in a significant fatigue life reduction relative to lower severity levels. However, systematic studies correlating ASTM nondestructive standards to performance are limited, 107 and to the knowledge of the authors, no other such quantitative standard has been proposed. Thus, estimated fatigue notch factors based on experimental data and coupled to a quantitative NDE standard provide a useful starting framework.

Figure  11  portrays the computed strain life curves against experimental data points from several low-alloy, high-alloy, and carbon cast steels in the literature dataset 86 , 90 , 94  using the proposed approach. The solid line indicates a fatigue notch factor of 1.0 (analogous to using the unmodified Roessle/Fatemi correlation), and the dashed line indicates a fatigue notch factor of 1.5 corresponding to Level I severity in Figure  10 . Strain life curves calculated using fatigue notch factors of 1.0 and 1.5 effectively bound experimental data across multiple alloy types and strength levels, indicating that the calculated fatigue notch factor of 1.5 for a Level I severity produces reasonably conservative lower bound estimates irrespective of the specific steel type. Figure 11 Calculated strain life curves for Level 0 (solid line) and Level I (dashed line) radiographic severity for several carbon, low-alloy, and high-alloy cast steels indicating the fatigue notch factor associated with Level I severity (K f  = 1.5) is generally conservative across multiple alloy types.

In Figure  12  summarizes the predicted and experimental reversals to failure for the cast steel dataset. Predictions made with the prior assumptions and the fatigue notch factor associated with a Level I severity result in reasonable predictions and are largely conservative with respect to the experimental data, particularly at longer lives associated with lower strain amplitudes, with the majority of the data falling conservatively within the 5x scatter bands. While conservative predictions exceeding five times the experimental fatigue lives may seem excessive, predictions utilize only the Young’s modulus, Brinell hardness calculated from the ultimate tensile strength, and a constant fatigue notch factor assuming Level I radiographic severity. Thus, with the least amount of experimental data available, the predictions should tend toward increasing conservatism. Such logic is already embedded within structural assessment procedures such as SINTAP, 108  which permits higher fidelity, less conservative assessments with higher analysis levels and more substantial experimental data. 109  The results of the present extension of the Roessle/Fatemi correlation and Blair quantitative NDE standard to cast steels are promising, regardless, as it enables fatigue life predictions by directly considering the alloy strength and indirectly considering its “quality” through the use of a radiographic-based fatigue notch factor. Figure 12 Predicted vs. experimental reversals to failure utilizing the Roessle/Fatemi relationship, compatibility equations, and fatigue notch factor of 1.5 corresponding to Level I severity.

Notably, all approaches predict non-conservative lives exceeding 10x for the 8630 microporosity specimens (not shown) and indicate that the proposed approach may not be compatible with this type of quality detail without additional modification (such as a larger fatigue notch factor). However, such a modification would not be supported within the framework based on quantitative radiographic measurement, and cases in which microporosity is prominent within a steel casting section may require higher fidelity approaches such as the finite element-based method proposed by Hardin and Beckermann. 110

sections.heading: Compatibility with Stress-Based Design and Generalized Fatigue Assessment Procedure
paragraphs: The proposed notch-based approach is also compatible with an allowable stress methodology similar to those in the AISC steel construction manual 111  and the ASME BPVC Sec. II. 112  Consistent with the compiled initiation life data discussed previously, analysis is restricted to fully reversed axial loading of a cyclically stable material, and complex geometries, multiaxial loading, or the presence of mean and residual stresses are not considered. By solving for the local strain and local stress sequentially, a nominal stress can be determined at a given fatigue life from the strain life curve estimated from the Roessle/Fatemi relationship and notch factor derived from Blair. Allowable stresses at 10 7  reversals (5x10 6  cycles) for severity levels 0 through 4 are summarized for a representative carbon (ASTM A216 WCB), low-alloy (ASTM A958 SC8630), and high-alloy (ASTM A743 CA6NM) steel in Table  4  (stresses are provided in ksi for consistency with the primary units in the ASTM material specifications). Interestingly, the calculated stresses between level 0 and level I correspond to 40% and 27% of the minimum tensile strength for A216 WCB, 35% and 25% of the minimum tensile strength for A743 CA6NM, and 35% to 24% of the minimum tensile strength for A958 SC8630. Thus, between level 0 and level I, the calculated allowable stresses for the three grades correspond to roughly 30% of the grade minimum tensile strength consistent with the allowable stresses in the ASME BPVC. 112 , 113  Considering the assumptions present and minimal data required in the proposed approach, the proximity of estimated allowable stresses to codified values offers a degree of reassurance in its rationale. For higher severity levels, the allowable stress decreases consistent with the exponentially increasing fatigue notch factor. The comparatively lower stresses at levels 3 and 4 is driven primarily by the function correlating the fatigue notch factor and severity level (Figure  10 ) and would vary if a different function were used. However, the comparisons in the previous section suggest that the fitted correlation is reasonable between levels 0 and 1, and the reductions in stress at higher levels could be considered comparable to those stipulated for “decreasing quality” connection details in the AISC construction manual (i.e., although a direct comparison cannot be made, level 0 would be analogous to plain base material while level 4 might correlate to a thick cover plate weld.) The notch-based approach is also compatible with generalized fracture mechanics-based procedures such as that illustrated by Batson et al. 13  Figure  13 a illustrates the Batson model, comparing experimental cycles to failure from load-controlled axial fatigue testing on 19-mm-diameter specimens extracted from a large OEM casting made to ASTM A487 Gr. 10B specifications. LEFM-based life predictions based on the ratio of the quality detail effective area to section thickness (a 0 /t) are overlaid to show the methodology from the original source. 13  Intuitively, fatigue life predictions become increasingly conservative with decreasing stress amplitude consistent with the transition of the dominant fatigue mechanism from crack propagation to crack initiation, and thus, the proposed approach can be integrated within the fracture-mechanics based framework to provide more refined, less conservative predictions as outlined subsequently. Figure 13 (a) Experimental stress range vs. cycles to failure with fracture mechanics-based predictions for various a 0 /t ratios overlaid as dashed black lines recreated from Ref.  13 . (b)Initiation, propagation, and total life estimated for OEM A487 Gr. 10B casting utilizing proposed approach.

The compatibility of the notch-based approach is best highlighted by treating the present comparison as a case study since all the critical inputs are included in the Batson study (primarily quantitative data on the quality detail determined via NDE.) The pertinent parameters for initiation life are estimated by first determining the Young’s modulus and ultimate tensile strength of the material (within the stress-based framework utilizing the Roessle/Fatemi correlation, the Young’s modulus cancels out and becomes a place-holder value but is included for consistency with the previously described strain-based formulation). Tensile tests conducted on specimens taken from the OEM casting indicate a Young’s modulus of 200 GPa and ultimate tensile strength of 870 MPa, which yields an equivalent Brinell hardness of 252 HB. Inputting these values into the Roessle/Fatemi relationship yields a fatigue ductility coefficient of 0.443 and a fatigue strength coefficient of 1296 MPa. Recall that the fatigue ductility exponent and fatigue strength exponent are constant values of -0.56 and -0.09. Inputting the strain life parameters estimated from the Roessle/Fatemi relationship into the compatibility equations yields a cyclic strength coefficient of 1477 MPa and cyclic strain hardening coefficient of 0.161. A suitable radiographic severity level must be determined prior to calculating the fatigue notch factor, and this is done utilizing the approximate 3.2 mm quality detail size detected by phased array ultrasound (PAUT) in the OEM casting. 13  The quality detail size over section thickness then yields an a 0 /t ratio of 0.17, which correlates to Level 1.7 severity and produces a fatigue notch factor of approximately 1.98. Although a uniform a 0 /t ratio of 0.17 is used presently, the a 0 /t ratio could also be handled on a more stringent case-by-case basis, or by using a maximum measured value for more conservative predictions. It should also be noted that while PAUT was used as the NDE method in the Batson model, calculation of the fatigue notch factor is identical to the radiographic methodology. The initiation life is then determined in terms of nominal stress by sequentially solving for the local notch strain and stress for a given number of reversals (subsequently converted to cycles), as illustrated by the dotted black line in Figure  13 b.

The propagation life is determined utilizing a fracture mechanics-based methodology consistent with the Batson model, and the reader is referred to 13  for additional details on the approach. The initial ratio of the crack size to section thickness is estimated by simply equating it to the radiographic severity level (treating the initiated crack as the same size as the initial quality detail). For example purposes, it is assumed that no experimental fatigue crack growth data for A487 Gr. 10B is available, and the crack growth rate defined by the Barsom upper bound for martensitic steels (Figure  3 ) is used (C=1.36*10 -10  and m=2.25). The fully reversed loading condition used for the experimental data presents some ambiguity regarding the appropriate stress range to use for calculating the stress intensity range in the Paris equation. For simplicity, only the positive portion of the stress range is used in the calculation of the stress intensity range, though there is also precedent for using the full range 13 , 114  (which would simply increase conservatism). Cycles required to propagate the crack through the section thickness are then calculated using the Paris equation and yield the dashed black line in Figure  13 b.

With the initiation and propagation lives determined in terms of the nominal stress strange, the total life is calculated by summation, yielding the solid black line in Figure  13 b. Figure  13 b illustrates that reasonable life approximations are achieved, with estimated lives generally within a factor of 5 of the experimental lives, and show only a modest increase in conservatism with increasing cycles to failure. Although the present comparison is limited, it illustrates reasonable life predictions of a cast steel within a stress-based framework derived solely from the Young’s modulus, tensile strength, and quality detail size from NDE. Thus, the example indicates that the designer may have some flexibility with regard to the design of steel castings for fatigue and can opt for varying degrees of conservatism by considering both the initiation and propagation life of the component.

All data presented in the present study (fatigue crack growth and initiation) are based on relatively simple geometries and load cases consistent with typical laboratory fatigue testing. While some specimens were extracted from real casting components, it should not be inferred that the performance from small tensile specimens corresponds to the performance of the material everywhere in the casting 113  any more than it would for a large forging. 10  Ensuring the casting meets its performance requirements without becoming cost-prohibitive ultimately involves a degree of collaboration and understanding between the design engineers, inspectors, fabricators, and end users. 115  As such, while the trends presented in this study may provide some useful guidance, the remaining facets of the casting lifecycle must be considered.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The present study reviewed crack initiation and propagation characteristics of cast steels from literature and established trends for estimating cyclic performance of steel castings. From this study, the following conclusions have been reached. Upper bound fatigue crack growth rates proposed by Barsom for wrought steels offer a reasonable approximation for ferrite-pearlite, martensitic, and austenitic cast steels based on the analyzed literature dataset. For increased conservatism irrespective of alloy type, the crack growth rates outlined in BS 7910 can be used. Fatigue crack growth threshold guidelines presented in BS 7910 and the ASME BPVC can be used as generally conservative estimates for long crack growth thresholds in cast steels. The thresholds provided by BS 7910 offer the most conservative lower bound. Strain life regression relationships developed predominantly from wrought steel datasets estimate non-conservative lives for cast steels. Implementing a uniform notch factor resulted in fair agreement with experimental data points for carbon, low-alloy, and high-alloy cast steels. A notch-based fatigue approach, derived from a quantitative radiographic standard proposed by Blair et al. and the Roessle/Fatemi regression relationship, indicated that Level 0 and Level I severity effectively bounded a significant portion of the literature strain life data in the present study. Allowable stresses calculated from the proposed approach between Level 0 and Level I severity exhibited a comparable ratio to the ultimate tensile strength of the material as those defined in the ASME BPVC (approximately 30%). The application of the proposed approach was restricted to fully reversed axial loading on simple geometries (laboratory fatigue specimens). More complex geometries and loading conditions may require simplification of the load case or the use of numerical methods such as finite element analysis to determine an appropriate notch factor. Additional case studies should be employed to verify the proposed approach against a broader dataset (such as loading on real components that have been inspected via NDE), and additional experiments to this end are currently in progress by the authors. Accounting for the initiation life provided more refined, less conservative fatigue life predictions. Intuitively, a fracture mechanics-based approach in which the quality detail is treated at the outset as a crack should offer the most conservative life prediction. Additional study is needed to couple NDE methods for surface and near-surface quality details, such as magnetic particle or dye penetrant testing, to steel casting cyclic performance. Much of the fatigue crack growth data compiled within this review pertains to sound material. Some studies suggest that propagation characteristics may be less sensitive to the presence of quality details than the initiation characteristics, but additional data would enable broader characterization. The term “quality detail” was used consistently throughout the present study in lieu of “defect.” Although “quality detail” is a newer term and likely less familiar to the technical community than “defect,” it essentially describes something that may or may not hinder part performance. The majority of data published in the literature is not framed within a given set of performance requirements that would objectively dictate whether a component is defective or not, suggesting that the use of the more general term “quality detail” is appropriate.
